Yes. 

The manipulation of time in the story is exceptionally well-balanced and serves the emotional arc of the narrative. The author uses **compression of time** effectively in the beginning—summarizing Clara's general life split between Larchmont and Chelsea, and jumping from February to the cruise in spring—and again during the first three days on the ship, condensing them into a few paragraphs of habitual routines (breakfasts with Bear, card games by the pool) to quickly establish how Clara is accepted by the community. 

Conversely, the author **stretches time** for the story's most emotionally resonant moments. The afternoon on the fourth day with Mateo and the "White Party" on the fifth night are given significant narrative space. Most notably, the final slow dance between Clara and her dying father—which in "story time" lasts only the length of a single three-minute song—is stretched out with rich sensory details, dialogue, and internal reflection. This slowing down of the pacing mirrors the narrator's desire to hold onto her father and memorize every detail of him before he is gone, making the climax deeply moving.
